summary: Mission Link is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12, built for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Two players share one storm. Mission Control on Earth sees a real solar storm coming, from NASA's DONKI space weather records, and can use a telescope and a big wall screen to watch it. The Astronaut on a Moon or Mars base can protect the crew but cannot see the storm. They have to talk to survive. Every move costs power, crew health or safety, and messages take 3 to 14 seconds to reach the Moon and up to 22 minutes to reach Mars, so kids feel the delay. The game plays one of two real storms, the X5.8 flare of May 2024 or the M8.1 flare of May 2025. It explains what really happened when the level ends. It teaches that space missions depend on decisions made with incomplete information, shared between people far apart. It runs in a browser on one device, on two devices, or alone.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mission Link is a two-player co-op game. Mission Control (Earth) sees the storm and sends one warning before a 60-second clock runs out. The Astronaut (Moon or Mars base) cannot see the storm, waits for the warning, then walks Nova around the base to choose one move: raise a shield, shelter, save power or do science. Each move has a real cost in power. Too much radiation, no power or no crew health ends the mission. Surviving earns stars. At the end, a mission debrief explains the result and shows what really happened in the real storm.

HOW IT USES NASA DATA

Each level plays one real storm from NASA's DONKI database (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): the flare class sets the strongest wave and the cloud speed sets the fading wave. The game labels the records "Archived NASA data", never live. Automated tests check each storm against the saved NASA records. Facts shown to players link to their NASA source pages.

WHO IT IS FOR, AND IMPACT

Ages 7 to 12. A For teachers page has a 20-minute lesson plan and five discussion questions. It works with no account, no download and no install, on a phone held sideways, a tablet or a laptop. BLIP, the base robot, coaches each move and asks kids to predict what happens next.

CREATIVE PARTS

- A 3D world built from pixel art: the Moon and Mars are small round planets, and the characters and buildings are made cube by cube from the same sprites as the flat pixel map.

- Low gravity: on the Moon and Mars, Nova walks in slow, floaty hops.

- Mars warnings arrive one wave late, like real messages.

- Commander Sola's warnings show on the base as alarm lights and a lit path, even when they are wrong, so the Astronaut has to ask.

- A telescope screen in Mission Control shows the storm now and next.

- Original music, made in code, with a Music on/off switch.

TOOLS

React, Vite, Vitest, Supabase Realtime (two-device play), three.js (3D), Web Audio (sound and music), Web Speech (Read to me), Vercel (hosting), GitHub. The pixel art, the 3D models and the music are drawn or written in code, not taken from image or audio files.
